title: Fifth commandment: life and peace (CCC 2258–2317)
hook: respect for every life and the work of peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth commandment: children honor parents, and parents and leaders serve. Your line was honor flows both ways. Did your thank-you go out? A new week begins. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

Two brothers, at the very start of the Bible's story. One farms, one keeps sheep. Both bring offerings. One is accepted, one isn't, and the older brother's face falls. God warns him that sin is waiting at the door, and that he can master it. He doesn't listen. He invites his brother out into the field, and there he kills him. Then God asks Cain where his brother is, and Cain answers with a shrug: am I my brother's keeper? The fifth commandment begins in that field.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS, TWO OFFERINGS.` → `SIN WAITING AT THE DOOR.` → `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?`

segments.voice: The commandment itself is short. In the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not kill." The Catechism begins with why. Human life is sacred, it says, because from its beginning it involves the creative action of God, and it stays forever in a special relationship with him. God alone is the Lord of life. Back in the field, God tells Cain, in the Douay-Rheims: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth." Even a life no one else saw taken is heard. From there the Catechism walks through hard ground, carefully. It allows legitimate self-defense, and the duty of those responsible for others to protect them. It teaches that human life must be protected from conception, and it rejects euthanasia and suicide, while asking for prayer for those who have died by suicide and saying we should not despair of their salvation. Its current text calls the death penalty inadmissible. And it warns about scandal: leading another person to do wrong. Then it turns. It moves from killing to anger. Jesus, in the Sermon on the Mount, says that whoever is angry with his brother is in danger of the judgment. The commandment reaches inside, to the place where violence starts. And so the Catechism ends this section with peace. Not just the absence of war. It quotes Augustine: peace is the tranquility of order. And it calls peace the work of justice and the effect of charity. It even lists strict conditions before any war could be called just, and asks everyone to work to avoid war. Cain asked if he was his brother's keeper. The fifth commandment's answer, in Catholic teaching, is yes: every life, and every peace.
screen: `THOU SHALT NOT KILL.` · `LIFE IS SACRED: GOD ALONE IS ITS LORD.` · `FROM KILLING TO ANGER.` · `PEACE: THE TRANQUILITY OF ORDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make peace with someone. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind with whom there's something unsettled: a cold silence, a sharp word, an old grudge. You don't have to fix it in two minutes. Just picture their face without the argument attached. Ask what one small step toward peace would look like: a message, an apology, simply dropping the subject. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just wish them well, honestly, once. The bell holds the time.
Fifth commandment. Thou shalt not kill: respect for every human life, from beginning to end, and the daily work of peace, starting with anger. Today's word.
Your line: every life. Today, take the one small step toward peace you pictured, even if it's only a kind word. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics examine themselves on the fifth commandment before confession, including anger and grudges; the sign of peace at Mass, shared before Communion, puts the commandment into a gesture.

fork.setup: you're Cain. your brother's offering was accepted and yours wasn't. God warns you that sin is waiting at the door. what do you do?
options: master it, and go do well.
invite your brother out into the field.
fork.reveal: God tells Cain he can have dominion over sin. in Genesis 4, Cain doesn't: he takes his brother into the field and kills him.

original.note: Hebrew: the verb in Exodus 20:13, 'thou shalt not kill'.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't murder anyone.
what it means: every human life is sacred, and the commandment reaches into anger and calls for peace.
what a scholar hears: Abel's blood crying from the ground, Matthew 5's anger, and Augustine's 'tranquility of order'.

notes: CCC 2258–2317 paraphrased (copyrighted translation). Editor: 'crouching at the door' (modern-translation wording) changed to a paraphrase following Genesis 4:7; fork answer now the right choice (master sin) with the story's outcome in the reveal; scandal defined as CCC 2284 does (leading another to do evil), not 'harm'.

Editor pass 2: the hook screen still said 'crouching' after the earlier edit; now 'waiting', matching the spoken paraphrase of Genesis 4:7. Matthew 5:22 paraphrase moved off modern-translation wording ('liable to judgment') to the Douay-Rheims 'in danger of the judgment', in the teach and the match. 'A reason, not a rule' cut, since days 1112, 1124 and 1130 made the same turn.

Audit (y4 1122–1131): Exodus 20:13 and Genesis 4:10 match the Douay-Rheims (Challoner); Genesis 4:7–9 paraphrase ('present at the door', 'thou shalt have dominion over it', 'Let us go forth abroad') and Matthew 5:22 'in danger of the judgment' confirmed; CCC 2258, 2267 (2018), 2283, 2304, 2308 checked and found sound; no changes.
